Day 1
From Hotel: 3 min · 4 min → Ancient Arsenal of the Maritime Republic
1. Ancient Arsenal of the Maritime Republic
The medieval shipyard where the Maritime Republic of Amalfi built and repaired its war galleys. Two surviving stone aisles of pointed Arab-influenced arches and ten pillars now hold the Museo della Bussola e del Ducato Marinaro, tracing the city's seafaring heyday when it rivalled Venice, Pisa and Genoa.

3 min · 1 min → Amalfi Cathedral & Cloister of Paradise
2. Amalfi Cathedral & Cloister of Paradise
The Duomo di Sant'Andrea crowns a dramatic 62-step staircase above the piazza, its striped Arab-Norman facade ablaze with golden mosaic. Inside are bronze doors cast in Constantinople before 1066, the baroque crypt of St Andrew, and the serene 13th-century Cloister of Paradise with its interlaced Moorish arches.

3. Valle delle Ferriere
A lush state nature reserve climbing the gorge above the paper mills, where the Canneto stream tumbles in waterfalls past ruined ironworks and ancient mills. The sheltered valley shelters the giant fern Woodwardia radicans — a pre-glacial relict found almost nowhere else in Italy.
Open 24/7

22 min · 24 min → Museo della Carta
4. Museo della Carta
A 13th-century paper mill in the Valle dei Mulini, still making Amalfi's famous cotton-rag bambagina paper on original water-powered vats and hammers fed by the Canneto stream. The Milano family's working museum shows how the town built a second fortune on handmade paper.

From Hotel: 12 min → Grotta dello Smeraldo
1. Grotta dello Smeraldo
An emerald sea cave 7 km west of town, reachable by boat from the pier or by descending 450 steps from the coastal road. Inside, sunlight filtering through a submerged opening turns the sea floor a luminous jade green; a rowboat circuits the cave past a ceramic Nativity scene lowered here in 1956.

16 min → Atrani
2. Atrani
Italy's smallest municipality by area, pressed into a limestone cleft a 15-minute walk east of town. Medieval lanes climb past the domed Santa Maria Maddalena, the tiny Piazza Umberto I with its fountain, and a sandy beach where local families swim — entirely off the coach-tour circuit.
Read more
Open 24/7
~1 hr
Piazza Umberto I · Atrani
40 min · 16 min → Villa Rufolo
3. Villa Rufolo
A 13th-century Arab-Norman estate built by the Rufolo merchant family — tower, cloister, and terraced gardens spilling 350 metres down to the Tyrrhenian. Wagner set Parsifal's enchanted garden here in 1880; the same stage hosts the Ravello Festival's open-air concerts each July and August.

4. Villa Cimbrone
A medieval estate assembled in the early 1900s by English aristocrat Lord Grimthorpe, its 11-acre garden of hedges, temples, and pergolas ending at the Belvedere of Infinity — a terrace of marble busts at the cliff's edge with a panorama Gore Vidal called the finest view in the world.

Day 3
From Hotel: 13 min → Fiordo di Furore
1. Fiordo di Furore
A deep limestone ria carved by the Schiato stream, spanned by a single arched road bridge 30 metres above a pebble cove — despite the name, it is a drowned river valley rather than a true glacial fjord. A staircase of 200 steps drops from the bridge to the fishermen's cove and an abandoned net-house below.
Read more

~30 min
SS163 bridge · Furore
8 min → Church of San Gennaro
2. Church of San Gennaro
A parish church in the Vettica Maggiore quarter, its dome tiled in white-and-blue majolica rhombuses divided by gilded ribs. The west-facing terrace beside it is the coast's best sunset viewpoint — an unbroken sightline to Capri and the open sea, free and unmarked by any tour group.
Read more
Open 24/7
~30 min
Via San Gennaro 1 · Vettica Maggiore
38 min · 5 min → Marina di Praia
3. Marina di Praia
A pocket cove wedged between two cliff walls, still worked by the fishing boats drawn up on its pebbles rather than given over entirely to sun loungers. A path on the far side climbs to the Saracen-era Torre a Mare watchtower, and the cove is rated one of the coast's best shore-dive sites for its sheer underwater wall.

~45 min

28 min → Church of Santa Maria Assunta
4. Church of Santa Maria Assunta
Positano's parish church, its yellow, green and blue majolica dome gilding the skyline above the pastel houses that tumble down to Spiaggia Grande. Inside, a Byzantine Black Madonna icon behind the altar is the object of the town's biggest annual festival each 15 August.

Day 4
From Hotel: 9 min → Villa Romana
1. Villa Romana
A 1st-century Roman seaside villa excavated in the heart of modern Minori, its triclinium, cryptoporticus and a nymphaeum with the original wall niches still standing. The site sat buried under silt from the Reginna Minor stream until a 1932 storm exposed it, and it now anchors a small antiquarium of finds from the excavation.

26 min · 8 min → Collegiata di Santa Maria a Mare
2. Collegiata di Santa Maria a Mare
A 13th-century church raised over an earlier chapel to house a Madonna statue found on the beach in 1204, elevated to collegiate rank by Pope Julius II in 1506. Its yellow-and-green majolica dome was completed in 1863, and the crypt below holds the relics of St Clement alongside a small museum of sacred art.

21 min → Torre Vicereale
3. Torre Vicereale
A 16th-century viceregal watchtower fused onto an older Angevin tower, built after a Turkish raid to warn the coast by smoke and fire signal. Cetara below it is still a working fishing port rather than a resort town — the source of colatura di alici, an amber anchovy extract with roots in the ancient Roman garum, now a PDO product.

12 min → Duomo di San Giovanni Battista
4. Duomo di San Giovanni Battista
The 18th-century Baroque-Neapolitan cathedral of Vietri sul Mare, the Amalfi Coast's ceramics capital since the 15th century. Its 36-metre dome is tiled in hundreds of fish-scale majolica shingles in yellow, green and azure, made in the workshops of the town it crowns.

1. Pompeii Archaeological Park
A Roman city of 15,000 buried under six metres of ash when Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD, its streets, forum, baths, villas and body-cast victims preserved intact for eighteen centuries. Rutted chariot tracks still cross the paving stones, and the House of the Vettii's frescoes are among antiquity's most direct encounters with a single lost day.

Local Tastes
Limoncello
Amalfi's signature lemon liqueur, made by steeping the peel of the fragrant sfusato amalfitano lemons — grown on the terraced groves above town — in alcohol and sugar.
Pasticceria Andrea Pansa
Delizia al Limone
A dome of soft sponge soaked in limoncello and filled with lemon cream — the Costiera's most beloved dessert, perfected along the Amalfi Coast.
Pasticceria Andrea Pansa
Sfogliatella Santa Rosa
The shell-shaped layered pastry filled with semolina-and-ricotta cream and candied fruit, invented at the Santa Rosa convent in nearby Conca dei Marini.
Pasticceria Andrea Pansa
Scialatielli ai Frutti di Mare
Short, fresh egg-and-milk pasta created on the Amalfi Coast in the 1970s, classically tossed with the day's shellfish and tomato.
Trattoria Da Gemma
Food Delivery
No delivery platforms operate on the Amalfi Coast — the town's steep lanes and limited road access make door-to-door delivery impractical; order directly from local restaurants by phone or ask your hotel.

Worth Knowing

The Town That Ran on Water

Three of today's stops tell one quiet story: water. The same Canneto stream that still turns the hammers at the Museo della Carta once powered dozens of paper mills up the Valle dei Mulini — and it begins higher still in the Valle delle Ferriere, where it feeds the waterfalls and keeps the giant ferns alive. Amalfi traded on the sea, but it ran on the mountain water pouring down behind it.

And the Arsenal is the coast's quiet giant. A maritime republic that once rivalled Venice, Pisa and Genoa is now reduced to two stone aisles and ten pillars at the water's edge. Step inside, and the pretty cluster of lemon-stepped lanes you walked through briefly becomes the capital of a Mediterranean power.
